econ-beh-01-c2.text: (2017). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-01-c2.quote: Economics Laureate Herbert Simon developed the concept of bounded rationality – limited rationality – as a collective term for organisations’ and people’s cognitive limitations and simplified decision-making rules.
econ-beh-01-c2.claim: Herbert Simon (Nobel 1978) coined the term bounded rationality.

econ-beh-01-c3.text: Gregory Wheeler. Bounded Rationality. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-beh-01-c3.quote: Given a specification of what will count as a good-enough outcome, satisficing replaces the optimization objective from expected utility theory of selecting an undominated outcome with the objective of picking an option that meets your aspirations.
econ-beh-01-c3.claim: Instead of maximizing utility, decision-makers set an aspiration level, a satisfactory threshold, and pick the first option that meets it.

econ-beh-02-c1.text: (2002). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2002. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-02-c1.quote: Together with Amos Tversky (deceased in 1996), he has formulated prospect theory as an alternative, that better accounts for observed behavior.
econ-beh-02-c1.claim: Their prospect theory (1979) replaces EU with a model that fits the actual patterns.

econ-beh-02-c2.text: (2002). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2002. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-02-c2.quote: A striking finding is that individuals are much more sensitive to the way an outcome deviates from a reference level (often the status quo) than to the absolute outcome.
econ-beh-02-c2.claim: The first change is that people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, not as final wealth levels.

econ-beh-02-c3.text: (2002). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2002. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-02-c3.quote: Moreover, most individuals seem to be more averse to losses, relative to a reference level, than partial to gains of the same size.
econ-beh-02-c3.claim: The most famous finding: losses loom larger than gains.

econ-beh-03-c1.text: (2002). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2002. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-03-c1.quote: Under such circumstances, they rely instead on heuristic shortcuts or rules of thumb.
econ-beh-03-c1.claim: A heuristic is a mental shortcut for making judgments under uncertainty.

econ-beh-03-c2.text: Liam Delaney. Key Concepts in Behavioural Economics, Section 3: Judgement, Heuristics and Biases. UCD Behavioural Science and Policy, University College Dublin.
econ-beh-03-c2.quote: The median estimates of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations were for 25% and 45% for groups that received 10 and 65, respectively, as starting points.
econ-beh-03-c2.claim: The 10-anchor group gave a median estimate of 25%; the 65-anchor group, 45%.

econ-beh-03-c3.text: Liam Delaney. Key Concepts in Behavioural Economics, Section 3: Judgement, Heuristics and Biases. UCD Behavioural Science and Policy, University College Dublin.
econ-beh-03-c3.quote: Judging the probability of an event or the frequency of a class based on the ease instances can be brought to mind.
econ-beh-03-c3.claim: Availability heuristic: judgments of frequency or likelihood are based on how easily examples come to mind.

econ-beh-04-c1.text: (2017). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-04-c1.quote: In traditional economic theory this is described using discounting – the assumption is that both income and expenses reduce by a constant factor with every passing month or year. Using such an assumption, the ranking of two future alternatives will always remain the same.
econ-beh-04-c1.claim: Exponential discounting implies time consistency: a plan made today, evaluating future tradeoffs, will still be optimal tomorrow when reevaluated.

econ-beh-04-c3.text: (2017). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-04-c3.quote: However, as Odysseus’ dilemma demonstrates, it is possible to change your mind when choosing between two options. The explanation is that experiences that are close in time take up more of our awareness – we discount more rapidly early on.
econ-beh-04-c3.claim: Hyperbolic discounting causes a fundamental problem: preferences change over time as the choice approaches.

econ-beh-04-c4.text: (2017). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-04-c4.quote: Odysseus who, like his crew, wanted to return home to Ithaca, solves the problem by plugging the crew’s ears with beeswax and then tying himself to the mast, with strict orders to the crew to ignore whatever he says until they are out of harm’s way.
econ-beh-04-c4.claim: Ulysses tying himself to the mast.

econ-beh-04-c5.text: (2017). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-04-c5.quote: This insight has been used in the “Save More Tomorrow” programme, designed by Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi as a means of increasing individual occupational pension savings.
econ-beh-04-c5.claim: Auto-enrollment, employer match, and Save More Tomorrow programs (Thaler-Benartzi) reduce undersaving without restricting choice.

econ-beh-05-c2.text: Brigitte C. Madrian, Dennis F. Shea (2000). The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior. NBER Working Paper 7682.
econ-beh-05-c2.quote: Although none of the economic features of the plan changed, this switch to automatic enrollment dramatically changed the savings behavior of employees.
econ-beh-05-c2.claim: Madrian and Shea (2001) documented this dramatic effect.

econ-beh-05-c4.text: (2017). Popular science background: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2017. NobelPrize.org.
econ-beh-05-c4.quote: Among other things, this has led to the introduction of nudge units in several countries, including the UK and the USA, agencies that aim to reform public administration through the use of behavioural economic insights.
econ-beh-05-c4.claim: The framework has been controversial, but the UK's Behavioural Insights Team (the 'Nudge Unit') was founded on it, and most OECD governments now have similar units.

econ-beh-05-c5.text: Stefano DellaVigna, Elizabeth Linos (2020). RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units. NBER Working Paper 27594.
econ-beh-05-c5.quote: In the Nudge Unit trials, the average impact is still sizable and highly statistically significant, but smaller at 1.4 percentage points, an 8.1% increase.
econ-beh-05-c5.claim: Effects are often smaller than originally claimed (DellaVigna and Linos found ~1.4 percentage points of behavior change on average across nudges run at scale, far smaller than in published academic trials).
